title: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO BREAK THE CHAINS—BUT ROMANS 6 SAYS SOMETHING SHOCKING ALREADY HAPPENED
paragraphs: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO BREAK THE CHAINS—BUT ROMANS 6 SAYS SOMETHING SHOCKING ALREADY HAPPENED
What Romans 6 Really Teaches About Freedom From Sin—and Why Grace Was Never Permission to Stay in the Prison Jesus Died to Open
There is a terrifying kind of prison where the door is already open...
but the prisoner keeps sleeping inside.
Not because the chains are still locked.
Not because the jailer still owns him.
Not because freedom was never purchased.
But because after living in bondage for so long, the cell has started to feel like home.
Maybe that is why Romans 6 can feel so uncomfortable.
Because Paul does not speak to sin as though it were merely a collection of embarrassing mistakes that Christians should try harder to avoid.
He speaks about sin like a ruler.
A master.
A power that once demanded obedience.
And then Paul announces something so radical that many believers spend years trying to emotionally catch up with what Christ has already accomplished:
If you belong to Jesus Christ, sin is no longer your rightful master.
That does not mean Christians become incapable of sin.
Romans 6 itself would make little sense if that were Paul's argument. Why command believers not to let sin reign if sin were no longer something they could obey?
The Gospel promises something different—and far more profound.
The Christian can still be tempted.
The Christian can still stumble.
The Christian can still experience a vicious battle with the flesh.
But the person united to Christ is no longer required to obey the master who once ruled him.
There is a difference between being attacked by an old tyrant...
and still belonging to him.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction desperately.
Because perhaps you love Jesus, but there is something you keep returning to when nobody is watching.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Lust.
Gossip.
Dishonesty.
A secret relationship.
An uncontrolled temper.
Envy hidden beneath a smile.
The desperate need for approval.
Maybe your struggle has become so repetitive that you have quietly rewritten your theology around your defeat.
“This is just who I am.”
“I've tried before.”
“God knows my heart.”
“At least I'm not as bad as I used to be.”
“Grace covers it.”
And that last sentence is where Romans 6 walks straight into the room.
Because Paul anticipates the horrifying distortion of grace before we can make it.
“Should we continue in sin so that grace may increase?”
His answer in Greek is explosive:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
Absolutely not.
May it never be.
Paul refuses the idea that grace is permission to comfortably continue under the domination from which Christ came to rescue us.
Grace does not make peace with the prison.
Grace brings the prisoner out.
Paul asks:
οἵτινες ἀπεθάνομεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, πῶς ἔτι ζήσομεν ἐν αὐτῇ;
“How can we who died to sin still live in it?” — Romans 6:2
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not begin with, “Try harder.”
He begins with identity.
Something happened to you in relation to Christ.
Romans 6 repeatedly ties Christian freedom to union with Jesus—to His death, burial, resurrection, and life.

Paul says believers were baptized into Christ Jesus and into His death. He describes them as buried with Him so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead, they might walk in καινότητι ζωῆς — kainotēti zōēs, “newness of life.”
Not merely improved life.
Not religious decoration over the old life.
Newness of life.
Christianity is not Jesus helping the old you become slightly more respectable.
At the heart of Romans 6 stands something far more dramatic.
Paul writes that ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη—“our old man was crucified with Him.”
Read that slowly.
Crucified.
With.
Him.
The Gospel does not merely tell guilty people to clean themselves up so God might finally tolerate them.
Jesus Christ entered our death.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And those who belong to Him are so profoundly identified with Christ that Paul describes His death and resurrection as defining the believer's new existence.
That is why Romans 6 is not motivational self-help.
It is resurrection theology.
Your hope is not the strength of your willpower.
Your hope is a crucified and risen Savior.
Paul explains the purpose: the “body of sin” is rendered powerless so that τοῦ μηκέτι δουλεύειν ἡμᾶς τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ—we would “no longer be enslaved to sin.”
There is the scandal.
You may still hear the old master's voice.
But the old master does not possess the authority he once possessed.
Sin says, “Come back.”
Grace says, “You don't belong there anymore.”
Sin says, “This is who you are.”
Christ says your identity is now bound to Him.
Sin says, “You've already failed too many times.”
The Gospel points toward a bloody cross and an empty tomb.
And perhaps the tragedy is that some Christians keep begging Jesus to accomplish a victory that Romans 6 tells them they must begin living from.
Paul says:
οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς λογίζεσθε ἑαυτοὺς... νεκροὺς μὲν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ζῶντας δὲ τῷ θεῷ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
“So you too consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 6:11
That word λογίζεσθε — logizesthe matters.
Paul is telling believers to reckon, consider, account themselves according to what is true because of their relationship to Christ.
This is not positive thinking.
It is not standing in front of a mirror repeating something you desperately hope will become reality.
Paul grounds the command in what he has just declared about Christ.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
Death no longer exercises mastery over Him.
Therefore the believer must learn to think and live from the reality of union with Christ.
You do not defeat sin by pretending temptation does not exist.
You confront temptation from a new position.
“I may feel this desire, but this desire is not my lord.”
“I may hear the old voice, but it is not my king.”
“My past may explain some of my wounds, but it does not own my future.”
“My feelings may scream, but Jesus Christ is Lord.”
That is freedom.
And then Paul becomes intensely practical.
“Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body.”
There it is.
Do not let it reign.
The Greek uses the language of kingship: βασιλευέτω — basileuetō, from the verb meaning “to reign” or rule as king.
Sin wants a throne.
Your eyes can become territory.
Your hands can become territory.
Your sexuality can become territory.
Your mouth can become territory.
Your phone can become territory.
Your imagination can become territory.
Your money can become territory.
Your wounded memories can become territory.
So Paul tells believers not to keep presenting the members of their bodies to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but to present themselves to God as people alive from the dead.
Romans 6 therefore destroys another dangerous misunderstanding.
Freedom from sin does not mean freedom from obedience.
Everybody serves something.
Paul deliberately reaches for the uncomfortable imagery of slavery to make the point unavoidable.
Whatever you continually present yourself to obey becomes your master.
Sin promises independence.
Then quietly builds chains.
It whispers that pornography is freedom while teaching your eyes to consume people.
It calls bitterness self-protection while slowly poisoning your heart.
It calls greed ambition.
Pride becomes “knowing your worth.”
Gossip becomes “telling the truth.”
Sexual compromise becomes “following your heart.”
Revenge becomes “protecting my peace.”
Sin has always been brilliant at renaming chains.
But Jesus calls chains what they are.
Not because He hates you.
Because He loves you too much to bless the thing destroying you.
That is why Romans 6:14 contains one of the most breathtaking promises in the chapter:
ἁμαρτία γὰρ ὑμῶν οὐ κυριεύσει.
“Sin will have no mastery over you.”
Why?
Not because you finally developed perfect discipline.
Not because you attended enough church services.
Not because you memorized enough verses.
Not because God found people naturally stronger than everyone else.
Paul continues:
You are “not under law but under grace.”
Grace.
But do not misunderstand that beautiful word.
Biblical grace is not God smiling politely while sin destroys His children.
Grace forgives.
Grace rescues.
Grace transforms.
Grace brings us beneath a new Lord.
That is why Paul immediately rejects the next possible excuse: if we are under grace rather than law, should we therefore sin?
Again:
μὴ γένοιτο.
Absolutely not.
Grace is not a loophole.
Grace is liberation.
And this is where Romans 6 may become painfully personal.
Paul asks his readers to remember the “fruit” of their former slavery.
In other words...
Look behind you.
What did sin actually give you?
Not what did it promise.
What did it produce?
That secret addiction promised relief.
What fruit did it produce?
That affair promised affection.
What did it leave behind?
That bitterness promised justice.
What happened to your heart?
That lie promised protection.
What did it cost your integrity?
That compromise promised pleasure.
What happened when the moment ended?
Paul asks what fruit they received from the things of which they were now ashamed.
Then comes the devastating conclusion:
τὸ γὰρ τέλος ἐκείνων θάνατος.
“The end of those things is death.”
Sin sends invoices after the pleasure is gone.
Sometimes the invoice arrives as a shattered marriage.
Sometimes as a damaged conscience.
Sometimes as a relationship you can never completely repair.
Sometimes as years spent feeding an appetite that became increasingly difficult to satisfy.
Sometimes nobody else ever discovers it.
But you know.
God knows.
And perhaps that is the place where shame has convinced you to hide.
But listen carefully.
Romans 6 was not written to convince hopeless sinners that they are too filthy for Jesus.
It was written to announce that Christ is a better Master.
The chapter does not end with shame.
It moves toward sanctification.
Toward eternal life.
Toward God.
Paul writes that believers have been freed from sin and have become servants of God, with fruit leading to holiness and its end eternal life.
And then comes perhaps the most famous sentence in the chapter:
τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος, τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.
“For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Romans 6:23
Look at the contrast.
ὀψώνια — opsōnia.
Wages.
Something earned. Something paid.
Then:
χάρισμα — charisma.
Gift.
Sin pays wages.
God gives a gift.
We earned death.
God offers life.
We brought rebellion.
Christ brought His cross.
We brought guilt.
Christ shed His blood.
We brought the scandal.
Jesus brought grace.
And this is where Christianity separates itself from every fantasy that says you can save yourself by becoming impressive enough for God.
You cannot purchase eternal life with religious performance.
You cannot erase yesterday with tomorrow's good behavior.
You cannot pray enough prayers to make the cross unnecessary.
You cannot baptize yourself in enough tears to become your own savior.
Eternal life is God's gift ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — en Christō Iēsou.
In Christ Jesus.
That is where freedom lives.
Not in self-improvement.
In Christ.
Not in hiding your scandal.
In bringing your sin into the light and running to Christ.
Not in pretending temptation disappeared.
In learning that temptation no longer possesses the final word.
Maybe you fell again last night.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you deleted the history.
Maybe you erased the messages.
Maybe you washed your face before walking into church and smiled when somebody asked how you were doing.
Maybe people call you strong.
Maybe your family thinks you're fine.
Maybe you even serve in ministry.
But inside, you are exhausted from maintaining two versions of yourself.
Listen.
Do not use grace as permission to keep hiding.
Use grace as the reason you can finally come into the light.
Repentance is not God standing at the doorway waiting to humiliate returning sinners.
Repentance is turning from the grave toward the One who is Life.
Confess what needs confessing.
Cut off what needs cutting off.
Seek accountability where accountability is needed.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Stop feeding what you keep asking God to starve.
Stop protecting the doorway through which the enemy keeps entering.
Present yourself to God.
Your eyes.
Your hands.
Your thoughts.
Your sexuality.
Your money.
Your ambitions.
Your wounds.
Your phone.
Your browser.
Your relationships.
Your future.
Your body.
Your whole self.
Not because surrender earns salvation.
Because Jesus Christ is worthy of the life He redeemed.
And when you stumble, do not turn your failure into permission to surrender.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Fight again.
Not to persuade Jesus to love you...
but because the Gospel has given those who belong to Christ an entirely new reason to fight.
Perhaps somebody reading this has been thinking, “But you don't know how many times I've failed.”
No.
But Romans 6 knows what kind of Savior you have.
Christ did not rise halfway from the grave.
The stone was not partially rolled away.
Death did not negotiate shared custody of Jesus.
Christ rose.
And Paul anchors Christian hope there.
So stop introducing yourself spiritually by the name of the prison Jesus came to deliver you from.
You are not required to say, “This sin will always own me.”
You can say, “Jesus Christ is Lord, and I belong to Him.”
There may be battles ahead.
There may be tears.
There may be consequences from yesterday that grace does not magically erase.
There may be habits that require ruthless, Spirit-dependent obedience and years of renewed thinking.
Romans 6 does not promise effortless sanctification.
It promises something better:
Sin is not your rightful king.
Jesus is.
That means freedom is not doing whatever you want.
Freedom is finally being liberated to belong to the One you were created for.
The world says freedom means nobody owns me.
The Gospel announces the better freedom:
I belong to Jesus.
And strangely...
beautifully...
eternally...
serving Christ is where the slave finally discovers what freedom actually means.
Talk to God.
Name the sin.
Bring it into the light.
Turn from it.
Trust Christ.
You do not have to explain the details.
Just say, “pray for me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Come back to Romans 6 when the old master knocks.
Let them discover Christ.

Salvation cannot be bought. But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people, and sharing biblical truth can place it in front of someone who might never have searched for it themselves.
And don't keep the blessing inside Christian circles.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has drifted.
Invite the person who stopped going to church.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person quietly drowning in shame.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
But before you leave this article, remember the prisoner.
The one sitting inside an open cell.
Perhaps tonight you finally understand why Romans 6 refuses to let you call bondage home.
Christ did not die so that grace could decorate your chains.
He died and rose again so that those who belong to Him could walk in newness of life.
The old master may still shout your name...
but Jesus purchased the right to give you a new one.
